context: linear network · pipe-laying rate, pressure test & disinfection, live connection to the existing main

brief.intro: New to this project type? A potable water network carries drinking water from a reservoir or trunk main to every plot: large transmission mains first, then distribution mains in the streets, then house connections and meters. It is pressure pipe, so it does not need a fall — it follows the road at a fixed cover depth — but every length must pass a pressure test and then be disinfected and sampled before it may carry drinking water. The programme is driven by metres laid per day per crew, by the delivery of pipe, valves and fittings, and by the short permitted shutdown in which the new network is connected to the live main.

scope.name: Route survey & existing services
scope.desc: Topographic survey, trial pits and utility detection so the main avoids existing cables and pipes.

scope.name: Permits & traffic management
scope.desc: Road-opening permits, no-objection certificates and diversions for each road section.

scope.name: Transmission mains
scope.desc: Large-diameter ductile iron, GRP, steel or HDPE mains from the source or reservoir to the area.

scope.name: Distribution mains
scope.desc: Smaller mains in the streets forming loops, so each plot can be fed from two directions.

scope.name: Valves & chambers
scope.desc: Isolation, air-release and washout valves with their chambers, and district meter chambers.

scope.name: Thrust blocks & restraints
scope.desc: Concrete blocks or restrained joints at bends, tees and dead ends to hold the pipe under pressure.

scope.name: Fire hydrants
scope.desc: Hydrants at the spacing the civil defence authority requires, fed from the distribution mains.

scope.name: House connections & meters
scope.desc: Service pipes from the main to each plot boundary, with meter box and meter.

scope.name: Pressure testing
scope.desc: Hydrostatic test of each section at the specified test pressure, with leakage measured.

scope.name: Flushing, disinfection & sampling
scope.desc: Swabbing, chlorination, flushing and laboratory samples before the main may carry drinking water.

scope.name: Connection to the existing network
scope.desc: Tie-in to the live main during a shutdown agreed with the water authority.

must_get_right: Plan the pipe-laying as a production rate (metres per day per crew, by diameter) and check that pipe, valves and fittings arrive ahead of each crew — a crew with no fittings stops.
Do not backfill joints or cast final reinstatement before the section's pressure test is passed, unless the specification allows it — a failed test under finished road is weeks of rework.
Disinfection and laboratory sampling take days and can fail; give them real durations and allow one repeat cycle before the connection date.
The shutdown for the live connection is granted by the water authority for a fixed window — treat its application, approval and date as milestones on the critical path.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by road section and by main (transmission, distribution, connections), so metres laid, tested and disinfected can be read section by section.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Pipe laying runs on the standard site calendar; work in public roads may be limited to off-peak hours by the traffic authority. The live tie-in is a night or weekend shutdown on its own calendar, on the date the water authority grants.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Each section repeats the same chain: permit → trench → lay and joint → thrust blocks cured → pressure test → backfill and reinstate. All sections then feed the network-wide chain: flushing → disinfection → samples passed → live tie-in → handover. The critical path normally runs through the longest transmission main and then the disinfection and tie-in at the end.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Existing services are as shown by the survey and trial pits; road-opening permits are issued section by section in the planned order; water for testing and flushing is available from the authority; and the tie-in shutdown is granted on the assumed date.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

rows: Before each section is closed for testing

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Only a limited length of trench may be open at once in a public road. Dewatering is needed where the water table is above the pipe. Pipe-laying crews are the production resource and are sized by diameter (large mains need a crane or excavator lift for every pipe).

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: unknown existing services, a late permit for one road, pipe or valve delivery slipping behind the crews, a failed pressure test, and a failed bacteriological sample that forces a repeat disinfection. Contingency is held before the tie-in date rather than spread along the route.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by road section and by main; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the pipe-laying and testing crews — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
